extracted.intended_audience: creative writers, students of narrative theory, and general readers interested in plot archetypes
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and applying Christopher Booker's seven basic plots and related narrative patterns (the meta-plot and rule of three) as a framework for analyzing or constructing stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-Plot stages
rubrics_metrics.description: The meta-plot begins with the anticipation stage, in which the hero is called to the adventure to come. This is followed by a dream stage, in which the adventure begins, the hero has some success and has an illusion of invincibility. However, this is then followed by a frustration stage, in which the hero has his first confrontation with the enemy, and the illusion of invincibility is lost. This worsens in the nightmare stage, which is the climax of the plot, where hope is apparently lost. Finally, in the resolution, the hero overcomes his burden against the odds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these sequential stages as a template for dramatic arc: call to adventure (anticipation), early success/illusion (dream), first serious setback (frustration), climactic loss or lowest point (nightmare), and reversal/overcoming (resolution). The meta-plot frames the hero's progression toward resolution; examples across literature and film illustrate this progression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero centrality / development toward self-realization
rubrics_metrics.description: "However many characters may appear in a story, its real concern is with just one: its hero. It is the one whose fate we identify with, as we see them gradually developing towards that state of self-realization which marks the end of the story. Ultimately it is in relation to this central figure that all other characters in a story take on their significance. What each of the other characters represents is really only some aspect of the inner state of the hero himself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate stories by how clearly they center narrative significance on a single protagonist and how well other characters reflect aspects of the protagonist's inner state. The arc should show gradual development toward a defining end-state (self-realization, redemption, downfall, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcoming the Monster
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist sets out to defeat an antagonistic force (often evil) that threatens the protagonist and/or protagonist's homeland.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core elements: a clear antagonistic force, a quest or mission to confront it, and stakes involving the protagonist or their community. Examples provided: Perseus, Theseus, Beowulf, Dracula, The War of the Worlds, Nicholas Nickleby, The Guns of Navarone, Seven Samurai / The Magnificent Seven, James Bond, Jaws, Star Wars: A New Hope, Naruto, Harry Potter. Use this plot when the primary dramatic tension is confrontation with an external threatening force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rags to Riches
rubrics_metrics.description: The poor protagonist acquires power, wealth, and/or a mate, loses it all and gains it back, growing as a person as a result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pattern: initial lack/poverty → acquisition of status/wealth/mate → loss → recovery with personal growth. Examples: Cinderella, Aladdin, Jane Eyre, A Little Princess, Great Expectations, David Copperfield, Moll Flanders, The Red and the Black, The Prince and the Pauper, The Ugly Duckling, The Gold Rush, The Jerk. This plot foregrounds social/fortune change and character maturation.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Quest
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist and companions set out to acquire an important object or to get to a location. They face temptations and other obstacles along the way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key features: clear goal/object/location, ensemble or companions, episodic obstacles/temptations, progress toward goal as primary narrative engine. Examples: The Iliad, The Pilgrim's Progress, The Lord of the Rings, King Solomon's Mines, The Divine Comedy, Watership Down, The Aeneid, Raiders of the Lost Ark. Use for journeys that test values and resolve through successive trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voyage and Return
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist goes to a strange land and, after overcoming the threats it poses or learning important lessons unique to that location, returns with experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinct from the Quest by emphasis on a strange/alien environment and a return transformed by experience. Examples: Odyssey, Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, Goldilocks and the Three Bears, Orpheus, The Time Machine, Peter Rabbit, The Hobbit, Brideshead Revisited, The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, Gone with the Wind, The Third Man, The Lion King, Back to the Future, The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe, Gulliver's Travels, Peter Pan, The Epic of Gilgamesh, Ramayana. Use when the narrative's stakes are learning/adaptation from an otherworldly setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy (patternal definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Light and humorous character with a happy or cheerful ending; a dramatic work in which the central motif is the triumph over adverse circumstance, resulting in a successful or happy conclusion. Booker stresses that comedy is more than humour. It refers to a pattern where the conflict becomes more and more confusing, but is at last made plain in a single clarifying event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat comedy as a structural pattern: escalating confusion/misunderstanding resolved in a clarifying event that produces a happy conclusion. Note Booker's claim that many romance films fall into this category. Examples: The Wasps, Aulularia, A Midsummer Night's Dream, Much Ado About Nothing, Twelfth Night, The Taming of the Shrew, The Alchemist, Bridget Jones's Diary, Four Weddings and a Funeral, The Big Lebowski.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist is a hero with a major character flaw or great mistake which is ultimately their undoing. The protagonist's unfortunate end evokes pity at their folly and the fall of a fundamentally good character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on an internal tragic flaw or mistake that precipitates downfall; emotional effect should include pity and recognition of the character's essential greatness despite error. Examples: Bonnie and Clyde, Carmen, Citizen Kane, John Dillinger, Jules et Jim, Julius Caesar, Macbeth, Madame Bovary, Oedipus Rex, The Picture of Dorian Gray, Romeo and Juliet, Hamilton, The Great Gatsby, Hamlet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebirth
rubrics_metrics.description: An event forces the protagonist to change their ways and often become a better person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot centers on an enforced transformation or moral renewal, often triggered by a crisis. Examples: The Frog Prince, Beauty and the Beast, The Snow Queen, A Christmas Carol, The Secret Garden, Peer Gynt, The Good Place, Groundhog Day, Iron Man. Use when the narrative emphasizes moral/psychological renewal.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Rule of Three (forms and function)
rubrics_metrics.description: The third event in a series of events becomes 'the final trigger for something important to happen.' In adult stories, the Rule of Three conveys the gradual resolution of a process that leads to transformation. This transformation can be downwards as well as upwards. Booker asserts that the Rule of Three is expressed in four ways: the simple (cumulative) three; the ascending three; the contrasting three; the final or dialectical form of three.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Four forms described: 1) simple/cumulative — e.g., Cinderella's three visits to the ball; 2) ascending — each event increases in significance (win bronze, then silver, then gold); 3) contrasting — only the third is positive (The Three Little Pigs); 4) final/dialectical — first two are wrong in opposite ways and the third is 'just right' (Goldilocks). Apply the rule as a structural device to pace escalation, contrast, or culminating transformation.
